'''Aryness Joy Wickens''' (January 5, 1901 – February 2, 1991) was an American [[economist]] and [[statistician]] who served as acting commissioner of the US [[Bureau of Labor Statistics]] and as president of the [[American Statistical Association]], and who helped develop the [[United States Consumer Price Index]].<ref name="wp">{{citation|title=Aryness Joy Wickens, ex-BLS deputy, dies|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=February 8, 1991|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1991/02/08/aryness-joy-wickens-ex-bls-deputy-dies/559b22dc-7a12-4a00-9de8-d4714126b6f4/}}.</ref><ref name="nyt">{{citation|title=Aryness Wickens, 90, Economist Who Developed Major Cost Index|first=Glenn|last=Fowler|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=February 8, 1991|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/02/08/obituaries/aryness-wickens-90-economist-who-developed-major-cost-index.html}}.</ref>

==Education and career==
Aryness Joy was born in [[Bellingham, Washington]]. She did her undergraduate studies at the [[University of Washington]], graduating [[Phi Beta Kappa]], and earned a master's degree in [[economics]] from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/>  At the University of Washington, she became a member of [[Kappa Kappa Gamma]].<ref>''The Key of Kappa Kappa Gamma'', v.39 (1922), p. 65</ref>

After teaching economics at [[Mount Holyoke College]] from 1924 to 1928, she moved to Washington, DC to work for the [[Federal Reserve Board]].<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/> There, her work included the measurement of [[industrial production]]. She also worked for a precursor of the [[Office of Management and Budget]] in the early 1930s.<ref name="wp"/>

Wickens joined the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 1933, at first serving on an advisory committee of the [[American Statistical Association]] to the program, and then working as an assistant to the commissioner of the bureau.<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/> Her work at that time involved the investigation of monopolistic business practices.<ref name="nyt"/>  She was promoted to branch chief at the BLS in 1940, heading a group that studied prices and the cost of living. Later Wickens became assistant and deputy commissioner of the bureau. During this time she also represented the US as an adviser at the [[United Nations]] and international conferences.<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/> In 1961 she became economic adviser to the Secretary of Labor. She retired in the early 1970s, but returned to duty at the Commission on Federal Paperwork as director of statistical studies there.<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/>

At the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Joy served as acting commissioner in 1946,<ref>{{citation|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9QA-AAAAYAAJ&pg=PP3|contribution=Letter of transmittal|title=Factors affecting earnings in chemistry and chemical engineering|volume=881|series=Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics|first=Cora E.|last=Taylor|year=1946}}.</ref><ref name="bls-com">[http://www.bls.gov/bls/history/commissioners/home.htm List of Commissioners and Acting Commissioners], [[Bureau of Labor Statistics]], retrieved 2016-07-18.</ref> and again in 1954–1955.<ref name="bls-com"/><ref>{{citation|title=The first hundred years of the Bureau of Labor Statistics|volume=2235|series=Bulletin of the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics|first1=Joseph P.|last1=Goldberg|first2=William T.|last2=Moye|year=1985|isbn=9780935043013|page=209|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XagWAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA209}}.</ref> In her second term as acting commissioner, her $13,500 salary made her the highest-paid female federal civil servant.<ref name="prescott">{{citation|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=897&dat=19541122&id=2ucKAAAAIBAJ&pg=4610,129980&hl=en|title=Highest Paid Career Woman At $13,000 Resides on Farm|newspaper=[[Prescott Evening Courier]]|date=November 22, 1954}}.</ref>

==Other activities==
In 1935, Wickens was considered as one of several candidates to be the president of [[Mount Holyoke College|Mount Holyoke]],<ref>{{citation|url=http://mtholyoke.cdmhost.com/cdm/ref/collection/p1030coll8/id/18254|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160815122630/http://mtholyoke.cdmhost.com/cdm/ref/collection/p1030coll8/id/18254|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 15, 2016|title=Letter from Alva Morrison to Amy Hewes|date=March 8, 1935}}.</ref> continuing a tradition of female leadership at that school. However, instead, controversially, the trustees selected [[Roswell G. Ham]] to be president.<ref>{{citation|title=A Male President for Mount Holyoke College: The Failed Fight to Maintain Female Leadership, 1934–1937|first=Ann Karus|last=Meeropol|publisher=McFarland|year=2014|isbn=9780786471331}}.</ref>

In 1952 she became the president of the [[American Statistical Association]].<ref name="nyt"/>

==Awards and recognition==
Wickens was elected as a [[Fellow]] of the [[American Statistical Association]] in 1937, the second woman (after [[Kate Claghorn]]) to be so honored.<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm List of ASA Fellows] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, retrieved 2016-07-16.</ref>

In 1960 Wickens was one of the inaugural recipients of the US [[Civil Service Commission]]'s Federal Women's Award.<ref name="nyt"/>

==Personal life==
Joy married [[David L. Wickens]], an [[economist]], [[United States Air Force]] lieutenant colonel,<ref name="wp"/><ref name="nyt"/> [[rancher]], and member of the [[South Dakota Senate]],<ref name="prescott"/> on June 29, 1935.<ref>{{citation|title=The Monthly Supplement: a current biographical reference service, Volumes 3–4|publisher=A.N.Marquis Company|year=1942|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nxcNAAAAIAAJ|page=171}}.</ref> Her husband died in 1970. After retiring, she moved to [[Mississippi]] in 1986.<ref name="wp"/>
